sm: The episode opens with a clip from the new film Confession, in which a character asks about the purpose of a confession and is told it cleanses the soul. The film was written by Ben Shapiro and stars Rob Lowe, James Franco and Nick Nolte, with acclaimed filmmaker Vaclav Marhoul directing. The host explains that he sat down in studio with Shapiro to discuss why he set out to make a Christian movie, what it was like working with an Oscar-nominated cast, and why the film's anti-communist and pro-Christian themes matter especially now. The hosts are John Bickley and Georgia Howe, in a weekend edition of Morning Wire.

Shapiro joins the show and the host says she has seen the film and is proud it is on the platform. Asked where the idea came from, Shapiro says he wanted characters who embody ideas through who they are rather than lecturing, and that as a student of Russian literature and Soviet history, he found a rich setting for that. Budgets at the company are low, and costs climb when a film moves between locations, so he challenged himself to shrink the setting to its barest essentials. The whole movie takes place essentially in two rooms.

He argues that constraints make for good art, contrasting this with unlimited budgets that produce computer-generated slop. The entire budget goes to the actors and director. The host agrees you feel the claustrophobia in every frame and says the writing is high level. Shapiro says he wrote the script in just four days, then watched actors spend months transforming into the characters, which he calls an honor.

Shapiro says he dislikes vanity projects, so he sent the script to people who would be honest with him. A well-known actor first wanted to play Vladimir but had a conflict. Shapiro then called Rob Lowe, whom he knew only slightly, to ask if he knew anyone who would work with them. Lowe read the first half, called an hour later in tears, and said the script felt like God touching him. Shapiro warned him the role, a broken-down, alcoholic Russian literature professor, meant playing against type, and Lowe was willing to go all the way. Shapiro calls it the greatest performance of Lowe's career.

They then sought a director, and the producer Dallas Sonnier went to Vaclav Marhoul, director of The Painted Bird, who loved the script. Lowe, also a producer, wanted it shot like Tarkovsky, using lighting and movement to keep a confined space interesting. James Franco joined after the original Vladimir actor dropped out, and Shapiro praises the whole cast, including Emile Hirsch, Richard Brake and Jennifer Jason Lee. He says every character should believe they are right, so viewers wonder whether the wife's pleas are correct, and the host admits she might have cracked.

Shapiro recounts Professor Robert George asking students whether they would have been abolitionists in 1853 Alabama, arguing that people must examine what they truly value. The host says the film builds tension through a series of conversations and does not leave viewers in darkness. Shapiro hopes people ask what values are worth living and dying for, what sacrifices they would make, and what courage means under pressure. The film takes up the meaning of life, the afterlife, and materialism versus spiritualism.

Shapiro says the film offers a robust, even offensive defense of Christianity, and the host calls it perhaps the most Christian movie she has seen and says everyone should watch it by age 18. Shapiro, who is Jewish, says he tried to be historically true and to speak in defense of every character, noting the overlap between Judaism and Christianity and that the people resisting tyranny in the Soviet Union in 1938 are Christians. Even characters he disagrees with, like Vladimir, must be convincing and fully human. The host notes everyone has an arc, and the conversation closes with congratulations.
sg: Writing a film in two rooms
